input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-101: Principles of Computing. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course is designed to introduce students to the central ideas of computing. Students will engage in activities that show how computing changes the world and impacts daily lives. Students will develop step-by- step written solutions to basic problems and implement their solutions using a programming language. Assignments will be completed both individually and in small teams. Students will be required to demonstrate oral and written communication skills through such assignments as short papers, homeworks, group discussions and debates, and development of a term paper. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 It may be used to fulfill one of the following: GE: Elective Typically Offered: Fall

Source excerpts:

[llvm-language-reference]
LLVM IR is a typed, SSA-based intermediate representation with explicit instructions, basic blocks, functions, memory operations, and control flow. A module contains global values, functions, declarations, and metadata. A function contains basic blocks, and every basic block ends with a terminator instruction. Phi instructions select values according to the predecessor control-flow edge. Load and store instructions make memory access explicit. Valid IR must satisfy structural and typing rules. The verifier reports IR that violates those rules. Compiler work separates parsing and semantic analysis from lowering, verification, optimization, and target-specific code generation.

[python-language-reference]
The Python language reference specifies lexical analysis, data model behavior, execution, expressions, statements, functions, classes, exceptions, and module import semantics. Python objects have identity, a type, and a value. Names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes. Expressions produce values, while statements control execution and bindings. Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate. The import system searches for modules and binds loaded modules into a namespace. Programs should be reasoned about through explicit state, control flow, data representation, contracts, tests, and observable behavior. Debugging separates syntax, runtime, and logical failures, while decomposition and abstraction reduce the number of interacting concerns.

This course is designed to introduce students to the central ideas of computing. Students will engage in activities that show how computing changes the world and impacts daily lives. Students will develop step-by- step written solutions to basic problems and implement their solutions using a programming language. Assignments will be completed both individually and in small teams. Students will be required to demonstrate oral and written communication skills through such assignments as short papers, homeworks, group discussions and debates, and development of a term paper. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 It may be used to fulfill one of the following: GE: Elective Typically Offered: Fall

beats.claim: CSCI-101 introduces the central ideas of computing and demonstrates how computing changes the world and impacts daily lives.
beats.example: Students will examine a short case study of how algorithmic sorting algorithms optimize data processing in modern search engines.
beats.title: Lesson Introduction and Course Scope
beats.visualDirection: Display a slide with the course title, a brief overview of the syllabus, and a graphic showing computing's impact on daily life (e.g., healthcare, transportation, entertainment).

beats.claim: Computing relies on the interaction between hardware, software, and data to process information and produce outputs.
beats.example: Students will trace how a simple calculator app uses hardware (CPU, memory), software (code), and data (numbers) to perform an addition operation.
beats.title: Hardware-Software-Data Relationship
beats.visualDirection: Show a diagram with three interconnected circles labeled Hardware, Software, and Data, with arrows indicating the flow of information between them.

beats.claim: Students will develop step-by-step written solutions to basic problems by breaking them into manageable, sequential tasks.
beats.example: Students will write a pseudocode sequence for a 'find the maximum number in a list' problem, listing each comparison and update step explicitly.
beats.title: Problem Decomposition and Sequential Steps
beats.visualDirection: Provide a template slide with numbered steps for pseudocode, highlighting the 'input', 'process', and 'output' sections.

beats.claim: Students will implement their solutions using a programming language, focusing on syntax, variables, and control flow.
beats.example: Students will write a Python script that declares variables, uses a loop to iterate through a list, and prints the maximum value.
beats.title: Introduction to Programming Language Basics
beats.visualDirection: Display a code editor window with syntax highlighting, showing variable declarations, a for-loop, and a print statement.

beats.claim: Python objects have identity, a type, and a value, and names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes.
beats.example: Students will compare integer, float, and string variables, explaining how each type affects data storage and operations.
beats.title: Data Types and Variables
beats.visualDirection: Show a table comparing variable types (int, float, str), their memory representation, and example assignments.

beats.claim: Statements control execution and bindings, while exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate.
beats.example: Students will implement an if-else statement to check if a user input is positive, negative, or zero, and handle invalid input with a try-except block.
beats.title: Control Flow and Conditionals
beats.visualDirection: Display a flowchart showing the decision path for an if-else condition, with arrows branching to true/false outcomes.

beats.claim: Functions and classes organize code into reusable components, reducing the number of interacting concerns through decomposition and abstraction.
beats.example: Students will define a function that calculates the average of a list of numbers, then call it multiple times in the main program.
beats.title: Functions and Abstraction
beats.visualDirection: Show a code snippet with a function definition and two separate calls, highlighting the reusable block.

beats.claim: Debugging separates syntax, runtime, and logical failures, while decomposition and abstraction reduce the number of interacting concerns.
beats.example: Students will run a test case with incorrect input, identify the error type, and fix the code to handle the edge case correctly.
beats.title: Debugging and Testing
beats.visualDirection: Display a split screen: left side shows the error message, right side shows the corrected code with comments explaining the fix.

beats.claim: Students will demonstrate oral and written communication skills through assignments such as short papers, homeworks, group discussions, and debates.
beats.example: Students will present their debugging process in a 2-minute group discussion, explaining the error, the fix, and the lesson learned.
beats.title: Communication and Collaboration
beats.visualDirection: Provide a slide with bullet points for a group discussion rubric, including sections for 'Problem', 'Solution', and 'Reflection'.

beats.claim: Students will apply durable concepts and problem-solving methods to evaluate their own and peers' code for correctness, readability, and adherence to course standards.
beats.example: Students will use a checklist to review a peer's Python script, verifying variable types, control flow logic, and error handling.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Display a printable checklist with boxes to check off: 'Variables declared correctly', 'Control flow matches problem', 'Error handling included', 'Code is readable and commented'.

learningObjectives: Students will define and explain the core concepts of computing, including the relationship between hardware, software, and data.
Students will demonstrate the ability to break down a problem into sequential, executable steps using pseudocode or a programming language.
Students will articulate how computing impacts daily life and the world, and practice oral and written communication through structured assignments.

State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.

Now define Hardware-Software-Data Relationship precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Expressions produce values, while statements control execution and bindings.
